item.title: The neurobiology of menopause: Implications for brain aging and Alzheimer's risk.
item.author: Mosconi L.
item.description:
A growing body of evidence implicates the menopausal transition as a neurobiological inflection point in women's brain aging and Alzheimer's disease (AD) vulnerability. Menopause is a midlife neuroendocrine transition characterized by a decline in sex steroid hormones and widespread systemic effects. The brain is not a passive recipient of ovarian hormones but an active endocrine-sensing organ. Menopause, however, does not act in isolation: the ovarian-brain axis is established embryonically, activated at puberty, remodeled during pregnancy and postpartum, and reconfigured during the menopausal transition, with implications for later-life brain aging. This review places menopause within a lifespan neuroendocrine framework, examining mechanisms by which the transition may influence the brain, including altered hormone signaling, bioenergetics, synaptic plasticity, neurovascular function, …

item.title: Glioma regulates GABAergic signaling to drive hyperactivity and tumor progression.
item.author: McDonald MF, Ko Y, Curry RN, Woo J, Ho R, He P, Puentes A, Yang Y, Latha K, Goethe EA, Lea ST, Seo K, Deng Y, Kim Y, Patel R, Basit Khan A, Yu K, Lu HC, Serin-Harmanci A, Noebels JL, Rao G, Deneen B.
item.description:
Recent studies have identified bi-directional communication between neurons and glioma tumors as a key driver of hyperexcitability and malignant progression. Although much of this work has focused on the activity of excitatory neurons, the roles of inhibitory neurons remain poorly defined. Using in vivo screening approaches in autochthonous glioma models, we found that the loss of a γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) transporter (Slc6a1) enhanced glioma progression, promoted network hyperactivity, and influenced tonic GABA release by tumors. Mechanistically, we show that glioma tumors influence the activity of inhibitory neurons and that their subsequent stimulation suppresses tumor growth. item.title: Trait-linked brainstem circuit resilience balances tau pathology-induced cellular vulnerability in Alzheimer's disease.
item.author: Zheng JQ, Fan HW, Yao C, Lai C, Yang CQ, Chen JJ, Liu ZQ, Zhou CW, Zhong Y, Xiong W, Zheng K, Guo Z, Man HY, Tang ZP, Shu K, Lu YM, Liu D, Zhu LQ.
item.description:
Although tau pathology correlates with cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease (AD), some individuals exhibit resilience by maintaining cognitive function. The mechanisms enabling this protection, particularly before widespread cortical degeneration occurs, remain elusive. Here, we identify a dynamic interplay between cellular vulnerability and circuit-level resilience that shapes cognitive outcomes in AD. Tau accumulation in the Edinger-Westphal nucleus (EW) impairs attention by inducing hypoexcitability in CART + neurons via Kcnma1 upregulation, a vulnerability predictive of future decline in both 3×Tg-AD mice and AD patients. Conversely, a subset of AD mice with heightened exploratory behavior activates a compensatory medial parabrachial (mPB)-EW circuit, mediated by substance P-Tacr1 signaling, which sustains CART + neuron function and delays cognitive deterioration. item.title: Remak bundle size, structure, and function are regulated by the Schwann cell basal lamina.
item.author: Lillis M, Yang C, Garcia ED, Pease-Raissi SE, Gould DB, McKemy D, Chan JR.
item.description:
Remak bundles are groups of small-diameter unmyelinated nociceptive axons ensheathed by Schwann cells (SCs). Whereas the development and maturation of myelinating SCs have been extensively studied, the formation of Remak bundles remains poorly understood. By preventing the secretion of type IV collagen from SCs, we observe normal myelin but abnormal Remak bundles. There is a decrease in Remak bundle density, an increase in bundle size, improperly ensheathed axons, and a decrease in mechanosensitivity. While Remak bundle formation appears to be independent of integrin signaling, the loss of type IV collagen leads to a decrease in postnatal SC proliferation. Inducing the emergence of supernumerary SCs rescues Remak bundle architecture and mechanosensitivity. item.title: A vagal gut-brain axis for feeding-induced gastric secretion in mice.
item.author: Wang Z, Tang Q, Li K, Li J, Mou J, Sun X, Wei Y, Chen Y, Guo P, Jin L, Liu B, Xiao B, Duan S, Dai W, Ni JD.
item.description:
Feeding begins with food-seeking and ends with nutrient absorption and waste elimination. Although meal-related sensory cues shape feeding behavior, how they engage neural circuits to control digestion remains unclear. We dissected vagal gut-brain-gut pathways mediating meal-induced gastric secretion. Stomach-innervating vagal afferents were necessary and sufficient for secretion. Among them, Glp1r + and Sst + neurons drove acid, pepsin, and gastrin secretion, whereas Oxtr + and Vip + neurons had little effect. Piezo2 was expressed in Glp1r + mechanosensory afferents, and conditional deletion of Piezo2 attenuated distension-evoked secretion. On the efferent limb, genetically defined vagal motor-neuron subsets showed distinct secretory effects: Cck + neurons broadly increased acid, pepsin, and gastrin, whereas Grp + neurons preferentially affected acid secretion. item.title: A GABAergic preoptic-raphe circuit mediates paradoxical coupling of anxiety and social preference after comparative social deficit.
item.author: Zhang YY, Hu MT, Xie SZ, Yu CX, Xu YH, Chen X, Tang MY, Li CY, Zhu Y, Hu JX, Tan LH, Wang H, Yang H, Yu YQ, Pan BX, Li XM, Lian H.
item.description:
Social disconnection is a major risk factor for anxiety disorders, the most prevalent mental illnesses worldwide, yet its neural substrates remain unclear. Here, we establish a comparative social deficit (CSD) model in adult male mice that induces a paradoxical phenotype of increased anxiety-like behavior together with heightened social preference, a pattern conceptually similar to human loneliness. Mechanistically, CSD increases the excitability of medial preoptic GABAergic (mPOA Gad2 ) neurons, which bidirectionally regulate CSD-induced behavioral changes. Transcriptomic and electrophysiological analyses identify downregulation of the Kv4.3 potassium channel (Kcnd3) as a molecular driver of mPOA Gad2 hyperexcitability. item.title: More than just accuracy: A pathway-level framework for implementing blood and digital biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease care.
item.author: Perneczky R, Schöll M, Rauchmann BS, Hofmann A.
item.description:
Blood biomarkers are transforming Alzheimer's disease diagnostics by enabling a scalable, minimally invasive assessment of pathology. Food and Drug Administration clearances and European market certifications of different plasma tests mark a shift toward biological diagnosis in routine care. However, clinical implementation is not guided by diagnostic accuracy alone but will depend on improved patient-centered and pathway-level outcomes, including diagnostic confidence, the appropriate use of CSF and PET assessments, time to diagnosis, amyloid-targeting treatment eligibility assessment, and trial recruitment. Digital biomarkers may complement blood tests by providing repeated measures of cognition, speech, and mobility. item.title: An acetylcholine-inhibited sleep-active hippocampal interneuron orchestrates memory consolidation.
item.author: Feng Y, Dai Q, Fei X, Yang H, Jiang T, Liu Z, Ye L, Lin Z, Gao S, Hu R, Li X, Liu R, Peng W, Xu M.
item.description:
Memory reactivation during hippocampal ripples is critical for sleep-dependent memory consolidation. However, the molecular-to-circuit mechanism enabling sleep-predominant ripple generation remains unresolved. Here, we discovered that a sparse population of GABAergic interneurons in the mouse hippocampus specializes in gating ripple generation and memory consolidation. While all known genetically labeled hippocampal interneurons were highly active during wakefulness and rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep, genetic targeting of M2 acetylcholine receptor (Chrm2)-expressing neurons isolated a specific population preferentially active during non-REM (NREM) sleep and quiet wakefulness. These acetylcholine-inhibited interneurons inhibited the entire hippocampus in an infra-slow rhythm (∼0.015 Hz). item.title: Distinct patterns of whole-body coding in human motor cortex and posterior parietal cortex.
item.author: Kadlec K, Gamez J, Aflalo T, Guan C, Rosario ER, Pejsa K, Bari A, Pouratian N, Andersen RA.
item.description:
Traditional views of cortical motor areas hold that movements of different parts of the body, or effectors, are represented in distinct anatomical locations. The extent of overlap in effector representations has been a topic of debate for decades. We recorded from single neurons in hand areas of the motor cortex (MC) and posterior parietal cortex (PPC) of tetraplegic humans while they attempted movements across the body. We found a population response to every movement tested in both areas; however, the hand knob of MC more selectively responded to hand movements, whereas PPC represented all effectors strongly. item.title: Raphe nuclei in cognition: A network-level framework for behavioral-state control.
item.author: Khalighinejad N, Rushworth MFS.
item.description:
Adaptive behavior requires organisms to maintain, update, and switch between behavioral states as environmental conditions change. The raphe nuclei (RN), best known as a major source of forebrain serotonin, have long been linked to arousal, inhibition, patience, affect, and flexibility, but these functions have often been considered separately. Here, we argue that recent advances in circuit tracing, cell-type-specific manipulation, high-resolution neuroimaging and neurostimulation, and computational modeling support a more integrated view in which RN are embedded within distributed cortico-subcortical and neuromodulatory networks.
